notes.title: Start here: errors, security and tests in a reference React app
notes.body:
Bulletproof React is a reference architecture: a discussion-board app (`bulletproof-react/apps/react-vite`) built to show how a React codebase stays maintainable. This quest is about the parts that keep it trustworthy, using three chapters of `bulletproof-react/fable-docs/`:

1. `07-error-handling.md`: three layers that catch different kinds of failure.
2. `08-security.md`: authentication versus authorization, token storage, XSS, and role and policy checks.
3. `09-testing.md`: which kinds of test to write, and the mock server that makes them honest.

Keep these files open while you read: `src/lib/api-client.ts`, `src/app/provider.tsx`, `src/app/routes/app/discussions/discussion.tsx`, `src/lib/authorization.tsx`, `src/components/ui/md-preview/md-preview.tsx` and `src/testing/mocks/`. The chapters quote trimmed versions of real code; compare every snippet with the file. Each chapter ends with **Try it yourself** steps, and the quiz asks you to predict what this code does in specific situations, so run at least one of them per chapter.

excerpts.quote: Errors *will* happen: networks fail, servers 500, code throws.

notes.title: Concept: which failures each error layer can see
notes.body:
Different failures surface in different places, so a robust app needs more than one safety net. Before reading chapter 7, sort these failure kinds: a request that comes back 500, an exception thrown while a component renders, an exception thrown inside a click handler, and a bug that only happens in a user's browser in production.

Then look for what in this repo is placed to see each kind:

- In `src/lib/api-client.ts`, read the error handler of the response interceptor to its last line, and think about what callers would see if that line were different.
- In `src/app/provider.tsx` and `src/app/routes/app/discussions/discussion.tsx`, find every `ErrorBoundary` and note exactly which components each one wraps.
- Look up in the React docs which kinds of errors an error boundary does **not** catch.

Chapter 7's "one story" section walks a single failure through all three layers; retell it in your own words.

readMore.why: The discussion route and its sections.

notes.title: Concept: client-side checks are UX, not security
notes.body:
Anything the browser enforces can be bypassed with DevTools, so the server must check every request. The client's checks exist so honest users see an honest UI. Chapter 8 separates two questions, *who are you* and *what may you do*, and shows two styles of the second: **RBAC** (decided by role) and **PBAC** (decided by a policy over the user and the resource).

Read `src/lib/authorization.tsx` from top to bottom; it is about 80 lines. As you read, answer:

- What does `useAuthorization` do before it returns anything?
- In `checkAccess`, what is returned for each possible `allowedRoles` value, including an empty array?
- How does the `AuthorizationProps` type constrain which props a caller may pass together?

Then open `md-preview.tsx` and trace a discussion body from string to DOM, and read the request interceptor in `api-client.ts` to see what it sets on every request. Chapter 9's MSW section explains how the mock server's handlers enforce the same rules on the "server" side.

readMore.why: The mock server rules for comments.

notes.title: Render errors go to the nearest boundary
notes.body:
An exception thrown while React renders a component unwinds to the nearest error boundary above it. In `discussion.tsx`, `<Comments discussionId={discussionId} />` sits inside its own `<ErrorBoundary fallback={...}>`, so that boundary catches a crash in any comment and renders its fallback.

- *The axios interceptor*: it only sees failed HTTP requests, not render exceptions.
- *react-query's isError*: it reflects a failed fetch promise; a render TypeError is not a query failure.
- *Sentry restoring the panel*: an error tracker reports errors; it does not render UI, and this repo does not configure one.

notes.title: Boundaries do not see event handlers
notes.body:
React error boundaries catch errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods and in constructors of the tree below them. An error thrown inside an event handler runs outside rendering, so no boundary catches it, including the app-wide one in `provider.tsx`. Chapter 7 says to `try/catch` a handler that can throw yourself.

- *The nearest boundary*: boundaries do not catch event-handler errors.
- *The app-wide boundary*: same rule; being the last resort does not change what a boundary can see.
- *The response interceptor*: it is attached to axios responses and never sees a synchronous click error.

excerpts.quote: Boundaries catch **render/lifecycle** errors only — not event handlers, not async code.

notes.title: The interceptor adds behaviour without swallowing
notes.body:
After adding the toast (and redirecting on 401), the handler ends with `return Promise.reject(error);`. The promise the caller awaits therefore still rejects: react-query records the error and sets `isError`, and a screen can react locally, for example by keeping a modal open. Returning normally would resolve the request with `undefined`, turning every failure into a fake success.

- *Toast after the caller handles it*: the toast is added before the rejection, unconditionally.
- *Retries once*: there is no retry logic in the interceptor.
- *Redirect before the toast*: the toast comes first in the code; order is not why it rejects.

readMore.why: The chapter on the classic interceptor bug.

notes.title: A section boundary limits the blast radius
notes.body:
The route renders `<DiscussionView>` outside the comments boundary and `<Comments>` inside an `ErrorBoundary` whose `fallback` is "Failed to load comments. Try to refresh the page." When Comments throws while rendering, only that boundary's subtree is replaced, so the discussion stays readable.

- *A full-page MainErrorFallback*: the app-wide boundary is reached only if no closer boundary exists.
- *A blank white screen*: that happens only with no boundary at all.
- *A toast and stale comments*: toasts come from failed requests; a render crash replaces the subtree.

excerpts.quote: Failed to load comments. Try to refresh the page.

readMore.why: Boundaries at both levels in this repo.

notes.title: With HttpOnly cookies the client only opts in
notes.body:
An HttpOnly cookie is set by the server and cannot be read by JavaScript at all; that is the protection against XSS token theft. The browser attaches it automatically, but cross-origin XHR only sends cookies when asked to, so `authRequestInterceptor` sets `config.withCredentials = true` on every request.

- *Copy it into a header*: impossible, because JS cannot read an HttpOnly cookie.
- *Keep a copy in localStorage*: that recreates exactly the XSS exposure the cookie avoids.
- *Sign requests with js-cookie*: js-cookie is used only by the MSW mock to simulate the cookie.

readMore.why: The chapter on why the client job reduces to withCredentials.

notes.title: Sanitize before dangerouslySetInnerHTML
notes.body:
`MDPreview` turns markdown into HTML with `marked`'s `parse`, then injects it with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(parse(value) as string) }}`. `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` bypasses React's escaping, so DOMPurify is what strips script tags and event-handler attributes.

- *React escapes it*: React escapes strings rendered as text, not HTML passed through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`.
- *The mock server strips tags*: the handlers do not sanitize bodies; their `sanitizeUser` only removes user fields.
- *A CSP in index.html*: no Content-Security-Policy is set in this app.

readMore.why: XSS and the markdown escape hatch.

notes.title: Ownership rules need a policy
notes.body:
"May this user delete this comment?" depends on *which* comment, so a role alone cannot answer it. `POLICIES['comment:delete'](user, comment)` returns true for an ADMIN, or for a USER whose id equals `comment.author?.id`. `comments-list.tsx` passes the result to `<Authorization policyCheck={...}>`.

- *allowedRoles set to USER*: that would show the button on every comment to every USER.
- *A server lookup in Authorization*: the component only evaluates the props it is given; it makes no request.
- *A flag stored on the comment*: comments carry an author, and the policy compares it with the user.

readMore.why: PBAC and how to choose between RBAC and PBAC.

notes.title: An empty roles list allows everyone
notes.body:
`checkAccess` filters only `if (allowedRoles && allowedRoles.length > 0 && user.data)`; otherwise it falls through to `return true`. With `allowedRoles={[]}` the length check fails, so `canAccess` is true and the children render for any signed-in user.

- *Nobody, no role matches*: no role is ever compared; the function returns true first.
- *Only admins by default*: there is no default role list.
- *TypeScript rejects it*: `RoleTypes[]` accepts an empty array.

readMore.why: RBAC as the chapter presents it.

notes.title: The props type forbids both at once
notes.body:
`AuthorizationProps` is `{ forbiddenFallback?, children } & ({ allowedRoles: RoleTypes[]; policyCheck?: never } | { allowedRoles?: never; policyCheck: boolean })`. An object with both props fits neither branch, because each branch types the other prop as `never`, so the call does not compile.

- *Both must pass*: the runtime code never combines them; and the call would not type-check anyway.
- *allowedRoles wins*: at runtime `policyCheck` would overwrite `canAccess`, but the type error comes first.
- *First prop wins*: JSX prop order does not affect the type check.

readMore.why: The chapter note on this technique.

notes.title: useAuthorization requires a user
notes.body:
The hook calls `useUser()` and immediately checks `if (!user.data) { throw Error('User does not exist!'); }`. It never builds `checkAccess` without a user. Components that use `Authorization` are therefore meant to render only inside protected routes, where a user is present.

- *checkAccess always false*: no `checkAccess` is returned when there is no user.
- *role undefined, access true*: the throw happens before any return.
- *Redirects to login*: redirecting is the protected route's job, not this hook's.

readMore.why: The user object as auth state.

notes.title: Mostly integration tests
notes.body:
Chapter 9's strategy in one sentence: mostly integration tests, a few unit tests for shared or complex pieces, and a thin layer of e2e tests for critical flows. An integration test such as `discussion.test.tsx` renders a route with the real router, react-query and form logic, with MSW standing in for the server, so one test covers routing, hooks, the API client and rendering.

- *Unit tests for everything*: they prove parts work alone; apps break at the connections.
- *E2e for every flow*: e2e tests are slow and flaky-prone, so they stay few, on money paths.
- *Snapshot tests*: the chapter warns against chasing such tests and coverage numbers.

excerpts.quote: **write mostly integration tests, a few unit tests for shared/complex pieces, and a thin layer of e2e tests for critical flows**

notes.title: MSW keeps the API layer in the test
notes.body:
Mocking `fetch` replaces the call itself, so the test never runs the API client, its interceptors or the query hooks' real requests. MSW intercepts real HTTP requests and answers them from handlers, so components send requests through the real `api` client and only the far end is fake. Here the handlers even implement auth and ownership rules over an in-memory db.

- *Skips JSON serialization*: requests are still real requests with real bodies.
- *Records and replays the real server*: MSW answers from handlers you write; it does not record.
- *A mocked fetch cannot return JSON*: it can; the problem is what it skips, not what it returns.
